title: Defence against disease
summary: How the body keeps pathogens out and destroys those that get in, how antibodies and memory cells give immunity, and how antibiotics, vaccines and herd immunity control infectious disease.

keyterms.definition: An organism or virus that causes infectious disease, e.g. viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.
Physical and chemical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes, that prevent pathogens from entering the body.
Sealing of cuts: platelets release clotting factors, triggering a cascade that converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh trapping blood cells.
Non-specific defences, present from birth and unchanged during life, that respond to broad categories of pathogen, e.g. phagocytes.
Specific defences, developed through life, in which lymphocytes produce antibodies against particular antigens and memory cells are retained.
A white blood cell that moves by amoeboid movement to sites of infection, engulfs pathogens by endocytosis and digests them with lysosome enzymes.
A white blood cell of the adaptive immune system; B-lymphocytes and helper T-lymphocytes cooperate to produce specific antibodies.
A recognition molecule, often a glycoprotein on a cell surface, that triggers production of a specific antibody.
A protein secreted by plasma cells that binds specifically to one antigen, helping to destroy or neutralise the pathogen.
An antibody-secreting cell formed when an activated B-lymphocyte divides to produce a clone.
A long-lived lymphocyte retained after infection that allows a faster, stronger antibody response if the same antigen is met again, giving immunity.
Human immunodeficiency virus: transmitted in body fluids, it infects helper T-lymphocytes, reducing antibody production and eventually causing AIDS.
A chemical that blocks processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells, so it kills or inhibits bacteria without harming human cells; ineffective against viruses.
An infectious disease that can transfer to humans from other animal species, e.g. tuberculosis, rabies and Japanese encephalitis.
A preparation containing antigens, or DNA or mRNA coding for antigens, that stimulates memory cell production without causing the disease.
Protection of a population when a high proportion is immune, so transmission chains are broken and epidemics are prevented.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only types of pathogen?
options: Bacteria, platelets, fungi
Viruses, antibodies, protists
Viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists
Phagocytes, bacteria, viruses
questions.explanation: Pathogens are organisms or viruses that cause infectious disease. Platelets, antibodies and phagocytes are part of the body's defences.

questions.statement: The skin and mucous membranes form the primary defence against pathogens.
questions.explanation: These barriers stop most pathogens from entering in the first place: the skin's tough outer layer is a physical barrier, and mucus traps pathogens.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of blood clotting in order.
items: A blood vessel is damaged
Platelets release clotting factors
A cascade of reactions converts prothrombin to thrombin
Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin
A mesh of fibrin traps blood cells, forming a clot
questions.explanation: The cascade amplifies the response so a clot forms quickly, sealing the cut against both blood loss and pathogen entry.

questions.text: Thrombin converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble ___.
questions.explanation: Fibrin forms long insoluble fibres that create a mesh, trapping red blood cells and platelets to form the clot.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the innate and adaptive immune systems.
options: Innate is specific to each pathogen; adaptive is non-specific
Both are specific and produce memory cells
Innate develops during life; adaptive is present from birth
Innate is non-specific and unchanging; adaptive is specific and develops memory
questions.explanation: Innate responses (e.g. phagocytes) attack broad categories of pathogen in the same way each time; adaptive responses (lymphocytes, antibodies) target specific antigens and improve with exposure.

questions.statement: Phagocytes take in pathogens by exocytosis.
questions.explanation: Phagocytes engulf pathogens by endocytosis, enclosing them in a vesicle; exocytosis is the release of materials from a cell.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of infection control by a phagocyte in order.
items: Phagocyte moves to the infection site by amoeboid movement
Phagocyte recognises the pathogen
Pathogen is engulfed by endocytosis into a vesicle
Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle
Lysosome enzymes digest the pathogen
questions.explanation: Phagocytes squeeze out of capillaries to reach infected tissues, then engulf and digest pathogens; this is part of the innate system.

questions.prompt: Match each defence to how it works.

pairs.right: Tough outer layer that pathogens cannot easily penetrate
Release clotting factors at a cut

questions.explanation: Skin and mucous membranes are the primary defence, clotting seals breaches, and phagocytes deal non-specifically with pathogens that get in.

questions.text: Mucous membranes in the airways secrete ___, which traps pathogens.
questions.explanation: Mucus is sticky and contains antimicrobial enzymes; it lines soft entry points such as the airways that are not protected by skin.

questions.prompt: How does blood clotting contribute to defence against disease?
options: It seals cuts in the skin, preventing entry of pathogens
It produces antibodies against pathogens
It digests bacteria with enzymes
It gives long-term immunity
questions.explanation: A cut breaches the primary defence; the clot quickly seals it, preventing both blood loss and pathogen entry.

options: A protein secreted by plasma cells
A recognition molecule that triggers antibody production
A white blood cell that engulfs pathogens
An enzyme that kills bacteria
questions.explanation: Antigens, usually glycoproteins or other molecules on cell or virus surfaces, are recognised as foreign and trigger production of specific antibodies.

questions.prompt: A person has blood group A. Which antigens are on their red blood cells and which antibodies are in their plasma?
options: B antigens; anti-A antibodies
A and B antigens; no antibodies
A antigens; anti-B antibodies
No antigens; anti-A and anti-B antibodies
questions.explanation: Group A red cells carry A antigens; the plasma has anti-B antibodies. Transfused group B blood would be recognised as foreign and agglutinated.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of antibody production in order.
items: A pathogen's antigen binds to a specific B-lymphocyte
A helper T-lymphocyte with the same specificity binds the antigen
The helper T-lymphocyte activates the B-lymphocyte
The activated B-lymphocyte divides by mitosis to form a clone
Clone cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies, and memory cells
questions.explanation: Only B-lymphocytes that are specific to the antigen and activated by a helper T-lymphocyte multiply, so large numbers of the right antibody are produced.

questions.statement: Each B-lymphocyte can produce many different types of antibody.
questions.explanation: Each B-lymphocyte produces just one type of antibody; that is why a specific B-lymphocyte must be selected and cloned for each antigen.

questions.text: Antibody-secreting cells formed by division of activated B-lymphocytes are called ___ cells.
questions.explanation: Plasma cells have extensive rough ER to secrete large quantities of a single antibody. Memory cells are long-lived but do not secrete antibodies until reactivated.

questions.prompt: Why is a second infection by the same pathogen usually much milder?
options: Memory cells retained from the first infection allow a faster, larger antibody response
Antibodies from the first infection remain in the blood for life
The pathogen cannot infect the same person twice
Phagocytes become specific to that pathogen
questions.explanation: Immunity is due to memory cells: they rapidly divide to produce plasma cells, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop. Antibodies themselves do not persist for life.

questions.statement: HIV is transmitted in body fluids, such as blood, semen and vaginal fluids, but not by casual contact.
questions.explanation: HIV is transmitted through sexual intercourse, shared needles, blood transfusion and from mother to baby, but not by touching, sneezing or sharing cups.

questions.prompt: Why does infection with HIV lead to AIDS?
options: HIV destroys red blood cells, causing anaemia
HIV makes bacteria resistant to antibiotics
HIV infects phagocytes only, so clotting fails
HIV destroys helper T-lymphocytes, so fewer antibodies are produced and opportunistic infections take hold
questions.explanation: As helper T-lymphocytes are lost, B-lymphocytes are not activated, antibody production falls, and infections that are normally controlled cause disease.

questions.prompt: Match each component of adaptive immunity to its role.

pairs.right: Secretes large amounts of one antibody
Long-lived cell giving a faster response on reinfection

questions.explanation: Lymphocytes cooperate: helper T-cells activate B-cells, which clone into plasma cells and memory cells specific to the antigen.
AIDS is a syndrome, a collection of diseases, that develops when HIV has destroyed so many helper T-lymphocytes that the immune system fails.

questions.prompt: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viruses?
options: Viruses are too large to absorb antibiotics
Viruses lack their own metabolism and use host cell processes, which antibiotics do not target
Viruses have thicker cell walls than bacteria
Viruses break down antibiotics with enzymes
questions.explanation: Antibiotics block processes specific to bacteria, such as cell wall synthesis. Viruses have no cell wall or metabolism of their own, so there is nothing for antibiotics to block.

questions.statement: Antibiotics can be used in humans because they block processes that occur in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells.
questions.explanation: Targets such as the bacterial cell wall or 70S ribosomes are absent or different in human cells, so bacteria are affected and human cells are not.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in the evolution of antibiotic resistance in order.
items: A few bacteria have a resistance gene due to random mutation
The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
The resistance gene is passed on to offspring
The proportion of resistant bacteria in the population increases
questions.explanation: This is natural selection: the antibiotic does not cause the mutation, it selects bacteria that already have it. Multiresistant strains arise this way.

questions.prompt: Which practice increases the spread of antibiotic resistance?
options: Completing the full course of antibiotics
Developing new antibiotics
Prescribing antibiotics for viral infections such as colds
Washing hands in hospitals
questions.explanation: Unnecessary antibiotic use, including for viral infections and in livestock feed, increases selection pressure for resistant bacteria without any benefit.

questions.text: An infectious disease that can transfer to humans from other animal species is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Zoonoses include tuberculosis, rabies and Japanese encephalitis. Most new infectious diseases in humans are zoonoses.

questions.prompt: Match each zoonosis to how it reaches humans.

pairs.right: Bite from an infected mammal such as a dog
Mosquito bite carrying virus from pigs or birds

questions.explanation: Each pathogen normally infects another species and crosses to humans by a particular route, which shows how these diseases can be controlled.

options: Antigens, or DNA or mRNA with sequences coding for antigens
Antibodies taken from another person
Antibiotics that kill the pathogen
Memory cells from a recovered patient
questions.explanation: Vaccines provide antigens (or the code to make them) so the body makes plasma cells and memory cells without suffering the disease.

questions.statement: mRNA vaccines contain the whole live pathogen.
questions.explanation: mRNA vaccines contain only mRNA coding for an antigen; body cells translate it to make the antigen, which triggers an immune response.

questions.prompt: How does herd immunity protect people who are not vaccinated?
options: Vaccinated people pass antibodies to unvaccinated people
The pathogen mutates and becomes harmless
Unvaccinated people develop memory cells by contact
When most people are immune, transmission chains are broken, so the pathogen rarely reaches susceptible people
questions.explanation: If a high enough proportion of the population is immune, each infected person passes the pathogen on to fewer than one other person, so epidemics cannot spread.

questions.prompt: In one region during the COVID-19 pandemic, there were 2000 confirmed cases and 50 deaths. What is the case fatality rate?
questions.explanation: Case fatality rate = deaths ÷ confirmed cases × 100 = 50 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 2.5%. Undetected cases mean the true fatality rate per infection is usually lower.
